articles.title: What could Chinese intelligence have learned from Nvidia CEO’s affair?
articles.summary: Nvidia says no secrets were compromised, but experts question what sensitive information may have been exposed.
articles.body:
United States lawmakers are pushing for answers from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid growing concerns over whether an affair he had compromised national security.

Huang, 63, has admitted to having extramarital relations during his time leading Nvidia, a major US tech firm. Media reports indicate the woman involved was Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed who is accused of working for Chinese intelligence.

As the scandal continues to grip Washington, Republican leaders of three committees in the House of Representatives have asked Huang to appear at a closed-door briefing to testify about the relationship.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast said he was prepared to subpoena Huang if he did not respond by the end of Wednesday.

According to The New York Times, US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the Nvidia CEO and influence him to push for looser restrictions on chip sales to China.

In a statement on Sunday, Jensen Huang apologised to his family and Nvidia employees about the affair.

His company also launched an independent investigation, saying it had no reason to believe that “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised”. Still, by Wednesday, media reports emerged that Nvidia was preparing to part ways with Huang over the controversy.

US President Donald Trump confirmed on Monday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was looking into the matter, but he has stood by Huang, calling him an “honourable guy”.

But the pressure on Huang intensified on Tuesday when Republican Senator Kevin Cramer called for him to resign.

“The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he’s got to go,” Cramer said in an interview with Politico.

But Huang, who co-founded Nvidia more than 30 years ago, has shown no signs of heeding that call.

Despite the company’s assurances, experts say the affair raises concerns about what information Alice Huang may have been privy to and what role the relationship may have played in the Nvidia CEO’s decisions.

What are the national security concerns surrounding Nvidia?

Nvidia’s advanced chips, which power much of today’s artificial intelligence, have put the company at the centre of the race for tech dominance between China and the US.

Since 2022, Washington has restricted sales of some of the most advanced chips to China over concerns that they could be used by the country’s military or intelligence agencies.

According to US intelligence officials cited by The New York Times, Alice Huang was tasked with getting Jensen Huang to lobby for looser restrictions on chip exports.

The Nvidia CEO had already been pushing for an easing of the rules, arguing that China’s domestic chip industry would get stronger without better access to US products.

But some experts say it is worth looking at how Alice Huang may have influenced decisions Nvidia made specifically about her former employer Megaspeed, which bought more than $4.8bn worth of Nvidia chips over the span of about two years.

Megaspeed has also been investigated over allegations that it helped Chinese companies get access to restricted chips. Megaspeed denies the allegation.

Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation who studies Chinese technology and intelligence activities, pointed to reports from Bloomberg and The New York Times that Nvidia contacted the US Commerce Department about its investigation into Megaspeed.

He also noted that, in disclosures to the government, Nvidia appeared to vastly undercount the value of the chips it sold to the company.

“The question at hand is whether Nvidia took specific actions with respect to Megaspeed that it might not otherwise have done,” Fedasiuk told Al Jazeera, “possibly as a result of the personal relationship between the two executives.”

What sensitive information could have been a risk?

There are also questions about what sensitive information Alice Huang may have had access to through her relationship with Jensen Huang.

In an analysis published by the Council on Foreign Relations, a think tank, senior fellow Jessica Brandt pointed to information about how Nvidia designs its China-specific chips.

“Information about its conversations with policymakers could be helpful for anticipating where those controls and other policies are headed,” she said. “Understanding where it disagrees with government could expose fault lines to exploit. And that’s before we get into anything touching R&D [research and development].”

Fedasiuk raised similar concerns about what Alice Huang could have learned about Nvidia’s internal operations and plans for future products, as well as its customer base, which includes American and foreign tech companies.

He also pointed to Jensen Huang’s close ties to Trump and other senior White House officials.

“I have to wonder what kind of information about those people and about those relationships may have inadvertently made its way to Ms Huang or to Chinese intelligence,” he said.

So far, however, there is no publicly available evidence that Alice Huang got access to sensitive information from Nvidia or influenced Jensen Huang’s decisions. US intelligence also has not made public any evidence that Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence.

China has flatly denied the allegations of espionage.

“The claim of so-called ‘Chinese spies’ is completely groundless and is nothing but a smear campaign against China,” said Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun on Monday.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV declares Peru his homeland as he arrives in Lima on a historic visit
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV described Peru as his “homeland” on Wednesday as he arrived in Lima for a historic visit, expressing gratitude to the people of the country
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV described Peru as his “homeland” on Wednesday as he arrived in Lima for a historic visit, expressing gratitude to the people of the country for shaping his journey as a pastor through their experiences, struggles and joys.Addressing president Keiko Fujimori and government officials after his arrival, the Chicago-born pontiff said the Peruvian citizenship he received in 2015 had strengthened a connection that had existed long before. In an emotional speech, he acknowledged the deep personal bond he shared with the country, according to news agency AP.“Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” Leo said, drawing applause from those present. “That is why I can tell you, with deep gratitude, that I am also returning to my homeland.”The pope received an enthusiastic welcome as he stepped off his chartered aircraft at Lima's airport, where he was greeted by Fujimori and embraced two children who presented him with flowers. According to the Vatican, nearly three million people lined the route of his motorcade into the capital, waving Peruvian and Vatican flags.Several enthusiastic supporters broke through security barriers to follow his vehicle as he travelled to the presidential palace for a private meeting with the president. During the formal welcome ceremony in the palace courtyard, Leo also sang the Peruvian national anthem alongside Fujimori and a children's choir.The Peru visit marks the final leg of the pope's three-country South American tour and its emotional high point. Before becoming pontiff, Leo, born Robert Prevost, spent more than two decades in Peru, serving as a missionary priest and later as a bishop. He has repeatedly credited the country with teaching him the meaning of pastoral leadership.Holding citizenship of both the United States and Peru, Leo is the first pope from either country.“We love him so much because he's worked here, he knows our sufferings, he knows it all,” said 85-year-old Evelina Cruz, who waited for his arrival carrying a stuffed toy of the pope made by her niece.Peru welcomes its beloved 'Padre Robert'Excitement surrounding the pope's return was visible across the country. Ahead of his visit, a 14-metre statue of Leo was unveiled in the port city of El Callao, while cafes in Lima began serving cappuccinos featuring his image.“My heart is so excited that it makes me want to cry with joy,” said Zuly Castillo, who previously worked as Leo's secretary when he served as bishop of Chiclayo in northern Peru.Gustavo Morello, an associate professor of sociology at boston college and author of lived religion in Latin America, described the visit as a return to the pope's roots.“Peru is the crown of the trip, the homecoming of the first Peruvian pope, no matter where he was born,” he said.Hundreds of people gathered outside the presidential palace in Lima, singing religious songs and chanting “Long live Christ!” as they awaited the pontiff.The enthusiasm has also spread to Chiclayo, where Leo is scheduled to arrive on Friday. Murals depicting the pope have appeared across the city, while his image features on T-shirts, baseball caps and bobblehead dolls.During the coming days, Leo is expected to visit several places associated with his years in Peru, including the sanctuary of St Turibius of Mogrovejo in Zaña, a centre of Afro-Peruvian culture. The pontiff frequently visited the sanctuary to pray to the saint, who holds a special place in his devotion.His familiarity with the country has heightened expectations surrounding his speeches, particularly an address scheduled for Thursday outside Lima's cathedral on the challenges and aspirations shaping Peru's future.Poverty, crime and political instabilityThe pope's visit comes as Peru faces several pressing challenges, including economic inequality, violent crime, political instability and the looming threat of climate disruptions linked to El Niño.The country, home to around 34 million people, recorded a monetary poverty rate of 25.7% in 2025.Morello pointed to the stark economic divide, saying a small wealthy elite enjoyed levels of prosperity comparable to those of some US states, while much of the population continued to face structural poverty and financial insecurity despite relatively strong macroeconomic indicators.Peru has also experienced a resurgence of violence and insecurity. Although the country is no longer confronting the insurgency of the Shining Path rebel movement that marked the 1980s and 1990s, rising crime has become a major concern.Rolando Pérez, a professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, said Leo's return as pope had generated considerable hope among people who felt neglected by the government.He said the pontiff was remembered as a religious leader who stood alongside ordinary citizens, brought their concerns into public discussions and supported their demands for justice.Amazon visit to highlight Indigenous concernsLeo is also scheduled to travel to Pucallpa in the Peruvian amazon, where he will celebrate mass and pay tribute to Indigenous communities.The region faces growing challenges from illegal gold mining and coca cultivation, which have affected Indigenous populations and their traditional territories.Pérez said the amazon brought together several major development concerns, including environmental degradation, the marginalisation of Indigenous communities, violence and extreme poverty.The pope will also visit Cusco, the historic capital of the Inca empire and an important centre of Spanish colonial rule. The city, known for its cultural heritage and proximity to Machu Picchu, will host a mass in its main square.The location carries historical significance as it was here that Indigenous resistance leader Tupac amaru II was executed in 1781 following a major rebellion against Spanish colonial authorities.Peruvians look to Pope for answersThe visit is taking place amid widespread public frustration over crime, corruption and political uncertainty.President Keiko Fujimori, who assumed office in July, came to power promising to restore order in a country grappling with rising extortion and homicides. The homicide rate has nearly doubled over five years, increasing from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people.Alonso Cardenas, a political science professor at Antonio ruiz de montoya university, said the pope's arrival coincided with a period of deep disappointment with political leadership. Peru has witnessed considerable instability over the past decade, with nine presidents taking office since July 2016.Rising insecurity and food prices have further added to public concerns.Cardenas said there was little indication that the government had developed an effective response to the country's growing security problems, prompting many Peruvians to look towards the pope for a message that could encourage political leaders to act.“There’s a profound sense of weariness regarding politics and corruption,” said Veronique Lecaros, head of the theology department at the pontifical catholic university of Peru.She noted that the catholic church continued to enjoy greater public credibility than other institutions in the country.Although catholic affiliation has declined in recent years, large crowds are expected to turn out for the pope's visit. According to the pew research center, the proportion of Peruvians identifying as catholic fell from 76% in 2013-14 to around 67%.Lecaros, however, said the decline did not necessarily indicate that Peruvians were abandoning their faith, with most continuing to identify as religious.She said Leo's visit could encourage some people to reconnect with the church, although its longer-term impact would depend on the conduct of catholic leaders and clergy.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran warns of expanded retaliation as Israel reportedly readies to attack
articles.summary: Israeli security cabinet orders military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran, Israeli media reports.
articles.body:
Israel has reportedly ordered its military to step up readiness for possible strikes on Iran as Tehran warned it would expand the war beyond the region if attacked.

Israel’s security cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the military to step up preparations for an attack on Iran, Israeli media reported on Wednesday evening.

“The directives issued by the security cabinet to the Israeli military could lead it to carry out activities that could trigger a war,” public broadcaster KAN reported.

KAN said the directives were made public after Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot issued a statement telling Netanyahu – who is serving as prime minister in a caretaker capacity – not to deploy the military “without a direct and immediate threat” until the next government is formed.

Eisenkot was offered the chance to form a new government by Israeli President Isaac Herzog over the weekend after Netanyahu’s ruling coalition lost its parliamentary majority in the October elections.

Netanyahu, who is on the cusp of losing power if the opposition succeeds in forming a government, has been adamant that the war on Iran will continue until the collapse of the government in Tehran.

Reports of Israeli preparations to attack Iran come at a time of intense diplomatic efforts to avert further conflict and reach a diplomatic solution.

US President Donald Trump has said that he is prepared to return to waging war if a diplomatic track offered by Qatar fails to facilitate a deal between Washington and Tehran.

Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei said in a social media post, “If the US launches another war against Iran, every military base involved in the aggression, from West Asia to Europe, will be a legitimate target for Iran’s lethal strikes.”

“No safe distance. No safe haven. No immunity,” he added.

Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas, reporting from Tehran, said the Iranian leadership has been discussing whether or not to appoint the hawkish Rezaei as Iran’s new chief negotiator.

“In Tehran, there have been voices saying that if this status quo goes on for quite a long period of time, Iran will not wait and might take pre-emptive action,” Atas said, adding that the current lead negotiator, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, has commented on Iran’s determination to move beyond this state of “no war, no peace” through “sustainable deterrence” if negotiations fail.

Ghalibaf told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview published on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz will “never return” to its status prior to the US-Israel war on Iran and that “the ball is now in the American court”.

“What stands in the way of an agreement is our lack of trust in the United States,” he said.

In Washington, DC, Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher said Trump is still justifying why he went to war with Iran and saying that it would end soon.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also said the Trump administration’s economic pressure campaign against Iran is proving so effective that a resumption of large-scale military operations is unnecessary.

“Over the last few days, both the president and Marco Rubio have said, effectively, that large-scale military engagement is over. They do not see the need to restart it unless Iran crosses red lines,” Fisher said, adding that the “key issue for this White House is always to be in a position where Trump can declare victory”.

“But it is clear there is some movement behind the scenes as far as negotiating a settlement,” he said.

Despite the push for peace, US forces “continue to work around the clock” in keeping the Strait of Hormuz open for commercial shipping, strictly enforcing the “ironclad” naval blockade against Iran, according to the US Central Command.

Meanwhile, oil prices rose about 1 percent on Wednesday after Tehran rejected a US proposal to transfer its stockpile of 60 percent enriched uranium to a third country.

Brent futures settled $1.27, or 1.39 percent, higher at $92.76, while US West Texas Intermediate crude gained 49 cents, or 0.57 percent, to $86.53.

In the previous session, oil prices had initially fallen by more than $3 a barrel after US officials played down the need for further military strikes against Iran.

Prices later pared some losses when an Iranian official said no talks were taking place between the two sides.

articles.title: Amnesty says UN, South Sudan officials failed to prevent village massacre
articles.summary: Peacekeepers knew of likely raid on Abiemnom, where more than 200 people were killed, according to rights group report.
articles.body:
United Nations peacekeepers and authorities in South Sudan failed to act on warnings before armed men attacked a village and killed more than 200 people earlier this year, Amnesty International said in a new report.

In the report, published on Thursday, the rights group said the UN mission, known as UNMISS, knew an attack on a village in Abiemnom, a remote area near the Sudan border, was likely, but did not reinforce its roughly three dozen peacekeepers there until after the March 1 assault.

The findings come as South Sudan heads towards elections next month that many fear could unravel a fragile peace.

“Both the government and UNMISS had sufficient information and time to take more effective preventive action. Their failure to take stronger action cost lives,” said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty’s director for East and Southern Africa.

Amnesty reported that between 1,000 and 1,500 armed men from the neighbouring Mayom County shot residents, burned homes, and looted part of the hospital. Authorities put the death toll at more than 200, including 130 town residents, 76 security personnel, and seven foreign nationals.

Satellite images showed more than 230 structures were burned, and most victims were buried in two mass graves, according to the report. Amnesty said the attack may have been triggered by tensions over earlier killings of several young men from Mayom County.

UNMISS spokesperson Priyanka Chowdhury said the mission did its best with limited resources to protect and treat about 2,500 people sheltering at a protected area it set up in anticipation of the attack. Facing budget cuts, it had “concentrated its available capacity on immediate protection of civilians seeking refuge within our base”, she said.

She said the mission had repeatedly asked the national army to send more forces after early warnings, and had known tensions were high since mid-February. UNMISS sent 40 more police after the attack.

Amnesty questioned why they were not deployed sooner, particularly after a similar deadly attack in April 2025.

The UN Security Council (UNSC) renewed UNMISS’s mandate in April, but cut its authorised troop ceiling from 17,000 to 12,000. Protecting civilians is a core task of the mission.

South Sudan is due to hold elections on December 22. On Tuesday, African Union envoy Jakaya Kikwete urged the UNSC to help ensure the vote is peaceful.

The International Crisis Group’s Murithi Mutiga warned that a rushed election could be “a final blow” to a 2018 peace agreement that had ended five years of a brutal civil war.

South Sudanese authorities did not respond to two letters from Amnesty requesting information and responses to the report’s preliminary findings.

The rights group called for an independent investigation into the killings and a separate review of the peacekeepers’ response.

“Behind every statistic is a story of devastation, death and destruction,” Chagutah said. “Abiemnom’s survivors deserve truth, justice and assurances that such a tragedy will never happen again.”

articles.title: Media industry could be forced by government to improve safeguards after David Walliams allegations
articles.summary: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy could force participation in an industry watchdog to protect whistleblowers, the BBC understands.
articles.body:
The government is prepared to force the entertainment industry to improve safeguarding practices unless rapid change is introduced, BBC Newsnight has learned.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy will tell a meeting of industry leaders next week that if their response to recent allegations is not robust enough, she is prepared to force participation in the industry body to protect whistleblowers, the BBC understands.

Participation in the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA) is currently voluntary.

It comes after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that entertainer David Walliams had been accused by several women of sexual misconduct and abusing his position, which he denies.

Nandy said earlier this week that she was summoning leaders from the broadcasting, publishing, film and entertainment industries to "draw a line" in the sand.

That announcement came after the publication of allegations against Walliams, as well as the sentencing of disgraced entertainer Russell Brand on charges of rape and sexual assault.

The allegations against Walliams were made as a part of a joint three-year investigation that was published after the entertainer lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public. Walliams denies all the allegations against him.

BBC Newsnight understands that the culture secretary will deliver two messages at next week's round-table meeting.

In the first instance, she will tell industry leaders that they need to meet the moment, take responsibility and tackle issues of safeguarding on their own. But she will add that if their response is not good enough, the government might have to intervene.

Intervention could include forcing participation in the CIISA.

Multiple government ministers gave statements on Wednesday that called for further restrictions on the use of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).

Women and equalities minister Bridget Phillipson told Sky News that there was "scope to go further" on legislation that restricted the use of such agreementsto ensure that the legal system was not being "abused in order to silence women".

"We cannot have a system where rich and powerful individuals - rich and powerful men - are able to silence women and stop things coming to light," she said.

Can't Buy My Silence founder Zelda Perkins told BBC Newsnight that there were "not enough safeguards" around high-profile people in creative industries and that joining the CIISA should be "mandatory".

The former assistant to jailed film producer Harvey Weinstein broke an NDA in 2017 when she spoke publicly about the movie mogul's mistreatment of women.

She has since founded a group that campaigns against NDAs being used in legal contracts or settlements to stop people from speaking out against their employers.

"There are no other regulatory bodies that are voluntary to join," Perkins told BBC Newsnight, referring to CIISA, noting that "obviously the people who need to be monitored are the people who are not joining".

"It's still very wild west in the the creative industries, people behave how they want," she said, adding that while "you can't change the humans, you can change the rules around them".

David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct after losing injunction bid

Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Brand

In the initial investigation published by the Guardian, some of the women accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault".

In a letter to journalists published by the paper, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

He said he "realised that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".

If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line .

Separately, a producer who worked on a TV show on which Walliams was a celebrity guest several years ago has told the BBC she was instructed to keep the comedian away from young female members of staff.

Speaking anonymously, she said she was warned that Walliams was "creepy" and "inappropriate", and that it was "well-known" he should not be put with young female runners.

She said she "wasn't at all surprised" when allegations about Walliams' behaviour emerged.

The Guardian reported that lawyers representing Walliams said he had never been warned nor "got into trouble" for messaging runners, and that he denied he behaved inappropriately and harassed young women in the workplace.

Comedian Kate Smurthwaite told BBC Newsnight that Walliams was a name that came up "over and over again", and that there was a "sense of worry" about him working with young people.

"People were saying that they knew people who had worked with him and either felt very uncomfortable and left, or stuck around and felt that his behaviour was inappropriate," she said.

When asked why it had taken so long for such allegations to emerge, Smurthwaite said: "We all know that women who raise these issues, there's a backlash, which might be legal, it might be in terms of your career or your opportunities, it might be as subtle as being seen as a problem."

articles.title: US government is proposing USCIS to bring a new rule that could mean thousands of employees on H-1B visa losing their visa approval
articles.summary: Thousands of H-1B visa holders and other foreign workers could face closer scrutiny when applying to extend their work status in the US under a new rule
articles.body: Thousands of H-1B visa holders and other foreign workers could face closer scrutiny when applying to extend their work status in the US under a new rule proposed by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The proposal would remove a regulation that requires US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to give weight to its own earlier approval when reviewing an extension filed by the same employer for the same worker and job. The proposed change could affect around 208,429 petitions each year, according to DHS estimates cited by immigration law firm Reddy Neuman Brown. H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN and E visa categories would be among those affected. The proposal was published on October 14, 2026, and public comments are due by November 13, 2026.Notably, the rule has not yet been finalized. The existing regulation will remain in effect unless DHS issues a final rule and it takes effect.What is DHS proposing to changeUnder the current regulation, USCIS generally gives deference to a previous approval when an employer files an extension involving the same worker, employer and underlying facts. An officer can move away from the earlier decision if there is a material error, a change in circumstances or new information that affects eligibility.DHS now wants to remove this requirement by deleting Section 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) and marking the paragraph as “Reserved.” If the proposal becomes final, USCIS officers would be able to review extension applications without being required to rely on the earlier approval. They could reconsider questions that had already been addressed, even if the worker remains in the same role with the same employer.The previous approval could still be considered, but officers would no longer be required to give it deference.Why DHS wants to end deference policyDHS says the current policy may shift the burden of proof from employers to USCIS officers. Under immigration law, the petitioner is responsible for proving that a worker qualifies for the requested status. The department also argues that deference could discourage officers from requesting additional evidence when eligibility has not been fully established. It says relying on an earlier approval could allow a questionable decision to influence future petitions.The deference policy was first introduced through a USCIS memo in 2004. USCIS rescinded the memo in 2017, reinstated deference in 2021 and DHS later codified it through the H-1B Modernization Rule in 2024, which took effect in January 2025.H-1B workers could face more requests for evidenceH-1B petitions account for more than 75% of all Form I-129 filings, according to DHS. This means H-1B workers could be among the most affected by the proposed change. The removal of deference could lead to more requests for evidence (RFEs) during routine extension applications. USCIS may ask employers to provide additional documents or revisit issues such as whether a job qualifies as a specialty occupation.DHS estimates that the proposal could result in around 6,044 additional RFEs each year. The agency’s analysis also found that denial rates did not statistically differ between periods when deference was in place and periods when it was not. More RFEs could increase the workload for both employers and USCIS, potentially leading to longer processing times.What could the change mean for workersIf the proposal is finalized, workers applying for extensions could face more uncertainty, even when their employment details remain unchanged. Additional evidence requests could delay approvals. Longer processing times may also affect workers who plan to travel abroad and need an approved extension before applying for a new visa stamp.Workers whose extensions are filed on time may generally continue working for up to 240 days after their I-94 expires while the application remains pending, subject to applicable rules. Longer processing times could bring more cases closer to this limit.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Bolivia arrests former judge on suspicion of drug trafficking
articles.summary: Arrests in Bolivia linked to a US-backed security alliance crackdown on drug cartels in Latin America.
articles.body:
Bolivian authorities say they have arrested a former senior judge on suspicion of drug trafficking, as part of a US-backed crackdown against officials involved in suspected cartel activity in Latin America.

Prosecutor Marcelo Inchausti told reporters that Aldo Quezada was arrested at his home in Santa Cruz in eastern Bolivia on Wednesday on suspicion of drug trafficking and criminal association.

Quezada had resigned last month as chief justice of the Santa Cruz departmental court after being named to a US visa restrictions list for alleged links to drug trafficking.

The United States has also cancelled the visas of officials in Colombia, Ecuador and Peru under the same policy.

Quezada is one of a number of senior Bolivian judicial officials to have been arrested since September on suspicion of having links to drug cartels, including former Attorney General Roger Mariaca.

Mariaca was arrested on September 30, also on suspicion of money laundering and drug trafficking, with police finding bundles of cash smuggled out of his house.

In September, the Trump administration imposed “visa restrictions on twelve Bolivian nationals and their families”, according to a statement by the US State Department.

Bolivia’s conservative President Rodrigo Paz assumed office on November 8, 2025, ending nearly 20 years of Movement for Socialism (MAS) governance, and has sought closer ties to the US.

Paz has signed his country up to US President Donald Trump’s “Shield of the Americas” , a new US-backed security alliance for the Americas.

articles.title: Fighting intensifies in Yemen as Houthis deny targeting Mecca
articles.summary: World Health Organization says more than 320,000 people have been displaced in Yemen fighting since August 1.
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthis have rejected Saudi claims that they targeted Islam’s holiest city, Mecca, as casualties surge in the war between the internationally recognised government and the Iran-allied Houthis.

A Houthi spokesperson on Wednesday denied what he called Saudi “lies” that the Iran-allied group had launched a drone towards Mecca, saying instead that a drone was launched at a pumping station in Yanbu on the Red Sea, and Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport was targeted with three cruise missiles.

Earlier, Saudi-led coalition forces said they had intercepted three cruise missiles launched towards Riyadh, along with drones launched towards Mecca and Saudi Arabia’s southern regions.

Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence Authority said debris from the interception of two ballistic missiles fell in the village of Sabuhah in Mecca province.

“This hostile targeting of civilian objects constitutes a flagrant violation of international humanitarian law and reflects the dangerous hostile approach pursued by the Houthi militia,” Saudi Arabia’s civil defence said early on Thursday.

Suspected Houthi missile strikes in the kingdom came as fighting intensified inside Yemen between the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of the internationally recognised government and Houthi fighters.

At least 138 Houthi fighters were killed or wounded in hundreds of targeted attacks, according to Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili, the spokesperson for Yemen’s army.

In a post on X, al-Nuzaili said Yemen’s Saudi-backed army had carried out 773 field artillery attacks on top of 44 drone strikes and 37 rocket attacks in al-Jawf, Marib, al-Bayda and Taiz governorates.

He also said Saudi-led coalition forces had conducted 23 air strikes against the Houthis, damaging 86 heavy weapons and military vehicles.

Despite their successes on the field on various fronts, the Saudi-backed forces have failed to stop Houthi attacks on the al-Buraiqa district in Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.

“The repeated shelling by the terrorist Houthi militia on the city of Aden, most recently targeting the densely populated al-Buraiqa district, reflects the militia’s established pattern of targeting civilians and terrorising innocent people,” Minister of Information Salem al-Awalqi said in a social media post.

“These assaults will fail to break the will of the people of Aden or undermine their resilience; rather, they will only strengthen their resolve to confront the aggression and defend their city,” he added.

Yemen’s Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said his forces had “successfully targeted” a Saudi coalition military command and control centre in Aden’s al-Buraiqa district with “several ballistic missiles”.

In a Telegram post, Saree said the facility was responsible for directing and overseeing Saudi military reinforcements across active fronts in Lahij, al-Dhale, Taiz and other governorates.

Casualties from the fighting in Yemen have risen sharply to 11,755, including 2,098 killed and 9,657 wounded, as of November 8, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The United Nations agency said that more than 2,000 casualties were recorded in just nine days, with Marib and Lahij among the worst affected governorates.

More than 320,000 people have been displaced as a result of fighting since August 1, including almost 16,000 forced to flee their homes in the past week, it said.

The WHO said strikes have also hit health facilities and ambulances, and warned that critical fuel shortages are disrupting emergency medical services in Taiz.

Despite the delivery of medical supplies and a vaccination campaign targeting nearly one million children, major gaps remain in trauma care, rehabilitation, and mental health services, it said.

articles.title: Ghanaian teen shot dead on way to school in New York; 17-year-old arrested
articles.summary: A 17-year-old teenager was arrested on Wednesday in connection with the fatal shooting of 15-year-old Ghanaian immigrant Javits Frimpong, who was killed
articles.body: A 17-year-old teenager was arrested on Wednesday in connection with the fatal shooting of 15-year-old Ghanaian immigrant Javits Frimpong, who was killed while walking to school in New york city, police said. The arrest comes amid growing demands for justice from the victim's family, Ghanaian officials and civil rights activists.The New york police department (NYPD) said the suspect had been taken into custody on murder and other charges in connection with Frimpong's October 29 death. Authorities have not disclosed the teenager's identity, and it was not immediately known whether he had legal representation, according to news agency AP.The killing has triggered protests across New York and prompted Mayor Zohran Mamdani to appeal to US president Donald Trump to facilitate a visa for Frimpong's mother, Doris Adu Gyamfi, allowing her to travel to the United States.“I need justice for my child,” Gyamfi said at a news conference on Wednesday before breaking down in tears.Police have not established a motive for the shooting, which took place on a Bronx street as Frimpong was heading to school. His family has alleged that he was being bullied by fellow students. NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny said last week that investigators were examining bullying and other possible motives, including robbery. He also indicated that three people may have been involved in the incident.The arrest was announced as Frimpong's relatives, civil rights attorney Ben Crump, reverend Al sharpton and Ghana's ambassador to the United Nations, Samuel Yao Kumah, gathered at sharpton's national action network headquarters for a previously scheduled press conference.Leading a chant of “Justice for Javits!”, Crump acknowledged the arrest but stressed that several questions remained unanswered.“What we're all wondering is: why? why did they kill this young man, this person with such a bright future?” he said.During the address, Frimpong's mother broke down and wept on Sharpton's shoulder.Kumah said the teenager's death had deeply shocked the Ghanaian community and described the arrest as “a step in the right direction”.According to his relatives, Frimpong had moved to the United States a year earlier to join his father and pursue better educational opportunities. His father, Thomas Frimpong, said the teenager had been “living the dream”.His sister, Millicent Frimpong, said he aspired to become a doctor and hoped to follow the family's tradition of serving in the military.“He was so ready that he made me save my uniform for him,” she recalled.She also revealed that her brother had written in his journal about how proud he was to be living in the United States and how well things were going at school.Thomas Frimpong had earlier said his son, who was generally quiet and spent much of his time on his cellphone, had been facing bullying at school. However, the teenager had reassured his father about the situation, telling him, “Dad, I’m OK.”The father also said two students had been suspended over the alleged bullying.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Blatant criminality': White House warns Democrats over planned investigations into Trump
articles.summary: The White House has warned the incoming Democratic chairman of the House Oversight Committee that investigations into the Trump administration could cross
articles.body: The White House has warned the incoming Democratic chairman of the House Oversight Committee that investigations into the Trump administration could cross legal boundaries and themselves become subject to scrutiny, news agency Reuters reported.In a letter sent on Monday to Representative Robert Garcia, who is set to take charge of the committee in January, White House counsel Will Scharf said the administration was "monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators". He warned that threats against government officials could be considered criminal."Threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality. And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation," the letter said.The warning comes after Republicans lost their majorities in both houses of Congress in last week's midterm elections. Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.Democratic leaders have vowed to investigate the actions of Trump, his family members, aides and advisers and hold them accountable.Scharf's letter accused incoming Democratic lawmakers of showing "a clear intent to transgress" constitutional limits on congressional investigations and subpoenas.It also referred to remarks by several lawmakers, including one Democrat who said subpoenas would be issued like "candy". The letter also cited an election-night post by Garcia on X that read "LAWYER UP."The comments "make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end," Scharf wrote.Responding to the letter on Wednesday, Garcia said the committee would continue its work despite what he described as threats from the administration."It appears Donald Trump has something to hide," Garcia said in a statement posted on the House Oversight Democrats' X page."The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers."The exchange comes days after Trump directed the US Justice Department on Saturday to investigate Democrats over what he described as threats against several people through impeachment and other forms of punishment.In a social media post, Trump called their actions a "criminal act" but did not provide evidence to support the claim.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1961, Soviet doctor Leonid Rogozov, 27, was the only physician at a remote Antarctic station when his appendix became inflamed; with no way out, he removed his own appendix in a surgery lasting nearly two hours
articles.summary: Leonid Rogozov was not simply stranded in Antarctica when appendicitis struck in April 1961.
articles.body: Leonid Rogozov was not simply stranded in Antarctica when appendicitis struck in April 1961. He was the only doctor at a remote Soviet research station, cut off by winter weather and frozen seas. With evacuation impossible and his condition worsening, the 27-year-old surgeon prepared an operating room, recruited colleagues to assist and made the extraordinary decision to remove his own appendix. The account was later documented in a 2009 British Medical Journal case report co-written by his son, Vladislav Rogozov.Rogozov was part of the sixth Soviet Antarctic expedition, which had sailed from Leningrad aboard the ship 'Ob' on November 5, 1960. After a 36-day journey, the team reached Antarctica and began constructing a new base at Schirmacher Oasis. The station, named Novolazarevskaya, officially opened on February 18, 1961. Twelve people would spend the long winter there, with Rogozov serving as their sole doctor. He also worked as a meteorologist and drove the station's terrain vehicle.The expedition had arrived just before the Antarctic winter set in. The ship had departed, the sea was freezing over and months of darkness, snowstorms and extreme cold lay ahead. The next resupply would not arrive for about a year, leaving the team largely dependent on its own resources.On April 29, Rogozov began feeling weak and nauseous. A pain in his upper abdomen gradually shifted to the lower right side, and his temperature rose. As a trained surgeon, he recognised the symptoms of acute appendicitis. He recorded his suspicion in his diary but initially kept quiet, not wanting to alarm his colleagues.The following day, his condition deteriorated. Antibiotics and other conservative measures failed to improve his symptoms. He developed a fever and began vomiting more frequently. An untreated inflamed appendix can rupture and cause peritonitis, a potentially life-threatening infection of the abdominal lining. Rogozov knew that he needed surgery, but an evacuation was not possible. Snowstorms ruled out flying, while the frozen sea and the distance from the nearest medical help made a return journey by ship impractical. He was left with an option few surgeons would ever contemplate: operating on himself.Rogozov converted his room into an improvised operating theatre, moving out furniture and keeping only his bed, two tables and a lamp. He selected a mechanic and a meteorologist to assist him. One would hand him instruments, while the other would hold a mirror and adjust the light so he could see the area he was operating on. A third colleague was kept ready as a backup in case either assistant became faint. He also prepared his colleagues for emergencies, showing them how to administer injections and provide artificial ventilation if he lost consciousness. After disinfecting the room and his assistants' hands, he positioned himself in a semi-reclining posture, with his right side raised.The operation began on April 30 under local anaesthesia. Rogozov injected the abdominal wall with Novocain, then made an incision measuring around 10 to 12 centimetres. He could not rely entirely on the mirror, which reversed the image, and had to use his sense of touch for much of the procedure.The surgery was far from straightforward. After about 40 minutes, he began feeling weak and dizzy, forcing himself to pause repeatedly. Sweat ran down his face, and he asked his assistants to wipe it away. During the procedure, he accidentally injured the caecum, part of the large intestine, and had to stitch the damage before continuing. He eventually located and removed the inflamed appendix, then closed the incision.The operation lasted approximately two hours, according to accounts based on his report and the contemporary Soviet record. Rogozov later estimated that the appendix might have ruptured within a day if it had not been removed.His recovery was closely watched by the station's small team. He continued taking antibiotics, his temperature returned to normal after five days, and he removed his own stitches after a week. Within about two weeks, he was back to his regular duties at the Antarctic base.The episode later became one of the most extraordinary accounts in the history of remote medicine. Rogozov returned to the Soviet Union in October 1962 and continued his medical career, eventually specialising in surgery. He died in Saint Petersburg on September 21, 2000, aged 66.His operation remains a striking example of the challenges faced by medical teams working in isolated environments, where even a common surgical emergency can become a fight for survival.You use AI every day. articles.title: I Swear author and TV stars among headliners for Clifton Lit Fest
articles.summary: More than 5,000 people are set to attend the event this weekend.
articles.body:
TV stars and BAFTA-winning authors are set to appear at a volunteer-run literary festival.

Bristol's Clifton LitFest, running from Friday to Sunday, was started by the Friends of the Clifton Library and has doubled in size since launching in 2019.

Taking place in shops and churches across Clifton, TV stars Mary Portas and Jonathan Porritt will appear alongside John Davidson, whose memoir was turned into the BAFTA-winning film I Swear.

TV presenter Jonathan Dimbleby, author and patron of Clifton Lit Fest, said he particularly likes that the event "belongs to the community". He added that its profits go to Bristol's libraries, giving the festival a "social purpose".

"Initially, it was the first and only literature festival in Bristol, which rather startled me.

"This is something that's very simple and straightforward, that involved people talking, listening, nuanced discussions with real people," added Dimbleby, who lives in Bristol.

Davidson said his talk will be "very eye-opening".

Speaking to BBC Radio Bristol, he added: "The amount of awareness-raising and more understanding achieved on the back of the film has been phenomenal.

"There's elements of it that are sad but there are also elements that can be inspiring and funny as well, situations I got myself in through having Tourette's."

In 2019, about 2,000 tickets were sold compared to 5,000 this year.

Rosalind Olsen, a volunteer who helps to organise the festival, said: "I think it's that point where suddenly it's on the map and people are now expecting it.

"There's almost a queue of people waiting for the programme to come out.

"Although it's big, it very definitely has its roots in community."

Olsen said they raised £10,000 last year, £5,000 of which they gave to the central library in Bristol and £1,000 to Christ Church and Hotwells schools.

"It's very definitely about the community supporting each other and giving back to the community," Olsen added.

articles.title: King's Lynn campaigners want more land protected from housing
articles.summary: After parkland was safeguarded from development, residents want the council to change a housing plan.
articles.body:
After a successful campaign getting parkland protected, residents in a Norfolk town are asking for more space to be given the same safeguards from development.

Seven acres (2.8 hectares) of land known as Harding's Pits, beside the River Great Ouse in King's Lynn, will be preserved after it was given "village green status" by the county council .

The Harding's Pits Community Association had campaigned for the past 30 years to keep the area as leisure space.

Next, the group wants the protection to be extended to the east side, which has been earmarked for up to 50 houses in King's Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council's local plan . The authority has been approached for comment.

Alexandra Kemp, an independent councillor, said she was asking her authority to amend its local plan.

She said: "I want to protect the east side of Hardings Way as a village green. To take out the 50 houses earmarked for Harding's Pits east from the borough's local plan, and provide community sports facilities, more trees and places for wildlife instead.

"Any development along Hardings Way risks more general traffic which would be devastating to the peace, quiet, safety, and amenity and wildlife."

The local council has been given a target to build more than 10,000 new homes by 2040 by the government.

Harding's Pits was turned into a public space in the early 1960s, but was originally a 19th Century clay pit which was then used as landfill.

The site is currently used for dog walking and as pedestrian access to King's Lynn town centre.

articles.title: 'Mithai khilao, you are Gujarat CM now': PM Modi recalls how journalists broke the news to him
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday recalled how a group of journalists once informed him that he had become the chief minister of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday recalled how a group of journalists once informed him that he had become the chief minister of Gujarat, asking him to distribute sweets.Addressing journalists at the BJP headquarters, PM Modi said only a few senior party leaders were aware of the development when a group of journalists walked into his room and told him, “You are the CM of Gujarat now, mithai khilao.”Recalling his journey with the media, PM Modi said he had witnessed its transformation from the days of press releases to the present era of Instagram reels. He also remembered his early days when he would arrange chairs at similar gatherings.PM Modi praised journalists for their role in keeping democracy vibrant, saying, “A vast diversity of thought sustains our democracy and keeps it vibrant—a process in which the Indian media plays a truly vital role.”Highlighting the dedication of field reporters, he said they often head towards disaster sites when others are moving away. “When a disaster strikes—be it an accident, an earthquake, or a devastating flood—while the rest of the world might flee from the scene, our field reporters head straight toward it... Such dedication is rare, and I have always held it in the highest regard,” he said.The prime minister also urged media organisations to highlight India's achievements and success stories, saying that considerable work was already being done in this regard. He called on journalists to spread awareness about the fight against drug abuse.Referring to India's ambition of becoming a developed nation by 2047, PM Modi drew a parallel with the importance of deadlines in journalism. He also thanked journalists for attending the gathering despite their busy schedules during the festive season, describing it as a “non-breaking news event”.The event was hosted by BJP president Nitin Nabin and attended by Union home minister Amit Shah, defence minister Rajnath Singh and health minister JP Nadda.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: The Australian in Indira's Tihar compound: When Sonia Gandhi carried lunch for Charles Sobhraj's accomplice
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: On Christmas Day 1978, Sonia Gandhi carried a home-cooked lunch into Tihar Jail for her imprisoned mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, and, at the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: On Christmas Day 1978, Sonia Gandhi carried a home-cooked lunch into Tihar Jail for her imprisoned mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, and, at the former Prime Minister's request, enough extra for a young Australian woman she describes as the accomplice of serial killer Charles Sobhraj.The episode appears in Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi's memoir, released on November 10. It is set in the week Indira Gandhi spent in Tihar after the Janata Party, the combined opposition formation, came to power in the elections that followed the Emergency. Sonia writes that she visited the jail daily during that period.Christmas, she recalls, had always been a special day in the household, especially for the children, even when Sanjay and Rajiv were little boys. "The celebration had no religious meaning for us, but it was a festive day when we exchanged gifts and decorated the house with colourful baubles and red poinsettias," she writes."But on this Christmas my mother-in-law was in jail. I felt that I had to do something special to keep our spirits up."A friend offered to send sliced ham with roast potatoes and a small Christmas pudding, while Sonia would prepare "a good soup and some vegetables". The plan soon had to expand."At my mother-in-law's request, the food had to be enough also for the three women who took turns guarding her and a young woman prisoner in her compound," Sonia writes. She identifies the prisoner as "an Australian girl, the accomplice of the dreaded Charles Sobraj, convicted for multiple murders of young tourists in Thailand, Nepal, and India"."My mother-in-law felt sorry for her," Sonia writes.Then came a hitch. "When it turned out that she didn't eat ham, we quickly had to change the menu and prepare a roast chicken instead."There was resistance from within the jail as well. The day before, Indira Gandhi had sent a note saying that "under no circumstances" should her daughter-in-law deliver lunch. Sonia was to have her Christmas meal with Rajiv and the children."I couldn't do it," she writes.She went to Tihar with the food, a book as a small gift, and cards from the children. "I rushed back rather late, but satisfied that I could celebrate with her briefly and also have lunch with Rajiv and the children," she recalls."As it happened, she was released the next day and came home."The passage offers a rare domestic glimpse into one of the most dramatic periods of modern Indian politics: a former prime minister in jail, her daughter-in-law shuttling between kitchen and cell, and a Christmas lunch stretched to include guards and a fellow prisoner linked to a notorious killer.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Record crowd greets Pope Leo as he calls Peru his homeland in emotional visit
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV was greeted by the largest crowd of his papacy in an emotional return to Peru on Wednesday, declaring the South American country where he served as a missionary for two decades his homeland.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV was greeted by the largest crowd of his papacy in an emotional return to Peru on Wednesday, declaring the South American country where he served as a missionary for two decades his homeland. The huge crowds, estimated at 3 million by local officials, pressed against police and security barriers, waving balloons and flags and chanting “Leo, Leo, Leo.” The pope was all smiles as he toured in an open-air popemobile and waved energetically on the final leg of his three-country, 12-day trip. In a closely watched speech to President Keiko Fujimori shortly after being greeted in Lima, the first Peruvian citizen to lead the Catholic Church urged the president to build confidence among her people after her narrow election victory earlier this year, and alluded to the contested legacy of her father, the late former President Alberto Fujimori. “This return visit holds a very special meaning for me,” the pope said at Lima’s Gran Teatro Nacional, mentioning many friendships made in his 20 years in the country and his love for a national dish, ceviche. “Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” he said. “I can tell you, with deep gratitude, that I am returning to my homeland.” Leo, originally from Chicago, is visiting Peru on the final and most personal stop of the most intense overseas trip by a pope in decades, after touring Uruguay and Argentina. The six-day visit is expected to include poignant scenes as the pope sees old friends and spends three days in the northern city of Chiclayo, where he was bishop from 2015 to 2023. Crowds lined the streets of the capital for miles to welcome Leo, evoking images of previous papal trips to Catholic strongholds like the Philippines, Mexico and Brazil. The main plaza in Lima, filled with people waving flags and wearing pope-themed shirts, erupted into loud cheers as a big screen showed Leo’s plane touching down. CamilaCerazo, 27, arrived with her toddler, husband and relatives, saying she hoped her son might someday remember the excitement surrounding Leo’s arrival. “Since people found out the pope had Peruvian nationality, they identified with him much more,” she said. Peru has prepared for the homecoming with fervor: a 46-foot statue depicting Leo with outstretched arms towers over a seaside park in Callao, while merchants in Lima are selling pope-themed shirts and souvenirs and inmates at the country’s largest women’s prison have stitched velvet dolls bearing his likeness. In the first of his scheduled 22 events in Peru, Leo urged Fujimori to confront the wounds of the country’s turbulent past, alluding to her father’s contested legacy. Alberto Fujimori was in office from 1990 to 2000 and spent many years in jail after leaving the presidency, convicted of human rights abuses. He was pardoned in 2017 and died in 2024. “Past events deserve to be treated with justice and sensitivity, leaving room for harmony to grow and for differences to be addressed with respect,” Leo said. Without referring directly to an internal conflict that lasted from around 1980 to 2000, Leo said Peru had endured “difficult times” that have tested the country. He called on Peruvians to cultivate “honesty, integrity, and a willingness to engage with others,” saying those qualities were essential to sustaining trust and democratic institutions. In her welcome to the pope, Fujimori said his visit was an invitation for Peru to pursue its “unfinished task“ of national reconciliation. When Alberto Fujimori was pardoned in 2017, Leo, then Bishop Robert Prevost, criticized the move, saying that the former president should personally seek forgiveness from victims if Peru was to achieve genuine reconciliation. Keiko Fujimori leaned heavily on her father’s political legacy during her presidential campaign, pledging uncompromising security measures to deal with rising crime. Ahead of Leo’s visit, Martin Cassinelli, an analyst at the Atlantic Council, said that any call for Peru to investigate its past would be unwelcome to President Fujimori. “If there’s anything that could potentially be at odds with the current Fujimori government, it would be a reflection on the past,“ Cassinelli said. Relations between the late Fujimori’s government and sectors of the Catholic Church were frequently tense, particularly over human rights during the state’s fight against the Maoist Shining Path insurgency. Church figures also opposed the 1995 amnesty for members of the security forces accused of rights abuses. A Vatican statement, citing local officials, said that 3 million people greeted Leo on his arrival in Lima, setting another record for the biggest crowd of his papacy after an estimated 2.5 million people attended an outdoor Mass he celebrated in Buenos Aires earlier this week. Leo ended the Argentina leg of his South American tour earlier on Wednesday with another outdoor Mass that drew a crowd of 2 million outside the shrine of Our Lady of Lujan, Argentina’s most important Catholic devotional site. The pope also visited one of Argentina’s largest penitentiaries, where he hugged several inmates and urged guards to treat detainees humanely. During his three-day visit to Argentina, Leo urged consideration for the disadvantaged at a time when the Church has criticized President Javier Milei’s austerity agenda for affecting the poor. Milei’s eyes welled with tears as he bade farewell to Leo on the tarmac, a surprising display of emotion from a president known for piling ​insults on Leo’s Argentine predecessor, Francis. Leo began the trip less than a month after lung cancer surgery and has appeared in good form, giving long speeches in a firm, clear voice.

articles.title: A Class 10 student from Kattappana in Kerala’s Idukki district has built a remote-controlled vehicle that lets farmers handle several farm jobs from a safe distance, and it has won him the state’s junior scientist award
articles.summary: Farming is the lifeline of India. It’s a fact. The occupation supports millions of livelihoods and plays a crucial role in the country's economy.
articles.body: Farming is the lifeline of India. It’s a fact. The occupation supports millions of livelihoods and plays a crucial role in the country's economy. Yet, the work often involves long hours of physical labour and is tedious. Understanding the issues, a class 10 student from Kerala has found an innovative way to make farmers’ task easy, combining technology and problem-solving to develop a multipurpose agricultural vehicle that farmers can operate remotely.Meet Anax Joshi, who is a young student from Idukki district. The young innovator has won the Bala Shastra Puraskaram (Junior Science Award), instituted by the Kerala State Sasthravedi, for his invention.Who is the young innovator?Anax studies at St Mary's High School, Vazhavara, in Kattappana. He has developed a remote-controlled vehicle aiming to help farmers carry out multiple agricultural activities without having to remain close to the equipment. His innovation has earned recognition for its potential to reduce physical labour, save time and make everyday farming operations more convenient.As per a report by Onmanorama, the young boy designed the vehicle to bring several farming functions together in a single machine. Instead of depending on separate equipment for different field operations, farmers can use the multipurpose vehicle to perform various tasks while controlling it from a safe distance.A significant inventionThe invention is particularly significant in a profession where many routine activities require considerable physical effort. From working in the fields to handling agricultural equipment, farming can be labour-intensive. His project explores how a relatively simple application of remote-control technology could help address some of these challenges.A practical idea rooted in the needs of farmersThe location matters. Kattappana, situated in Kerala's Idukki district, is surrounded by an agricultural landscape where cultivation is an important part of the local economy. The region is known for crops such as cardamom, pepper, tea, coffee and other spices. Agriculture in the district also includes a significant number of small and marginal farmers.For farmers, completing different agricultural operations often means spending long hours working in the fields and handling equipment. Depending on the nature of the work, these activities can involve considerable physical effort. The need to manage multiple tasks can also increase the time and labour required to maintain a farm.What is the vehicle’s purposeAnax's multipurpose vehicle attempts to address this challenge through a single technological solution.Its remote-controlled mechanism allows the operator to manage field activities without having to stay alongside the machine throughout the operation. This distance-based operation is an important aspect of the project, particularly when farmers need to avoid direct exposure to certain field conditions or equipment.The idea also reflects a larger shift taking place in agriculture, where technology is increasingly being explored to make traditional farming practices more efficient. Mechanisation, automation and remote-operated equipment are being considered as ways to reduce dependence on manual labour and improve the productivity of agricultural operations.Anax receives state-level recognitionAnax's work earned him the Bala Shastra Puraskaram, also known as the Junior Science Award, instituted by the Kerala State Sasthravedi. The recognition celebrates young minds who demonstrate scientific curiosity, innovative thinking and the ability to develop solutions to practical problems.According to Onmanorama, Anax is the son of Joshi Sebastian and Jaisy Joshi, who hail from Thundathil, Nalumukku. He is currently pursuing his Class 10 education at St Mary's High School, Vazhavara.It’s an encouraging recognition which matters a lot for a young student interested in applying science to real-world problems beyond textbooks. For Anax, winning the award is recognition of an idea that connects scientific curiosity with the needs of an important section of society.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: India bypasses own rules to buy Israeli phone-hacking tech
articles.summary: India’s expansive surveillance capabilities extend beyond cloning phones to accessing cloud-based data of tech giants.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – India has exempted an Israeli phone-hacking company from New Delhi’s own rules, allowing it to sell phone-extraction products and surveillance technology to government agencies and sparking concerns and criticism from rights groups and activists.

An investigation by the digital-rights group Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) found Indian Home Minister Amit Shah, a close confidante of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, signed off on exemptions from “make in India” procurement rules, clearing the way for government forensic institutions to buy at least 422 items of foreign technology, including products made by the Israeli firm Cellebrite.

Modi’s federal government and state governments ruled by his Bharatiya Janata Party are not the only ones who bought this Israeli technology. States governed by the opposition Indian National Congress party, including Himachal Pradesh, Keralam and Karnataka, also purchased similar phone-extraction and cloning tools.

A review of documents revealed that India’s expansive surveillance capabilities extend far beyond just cloning phones and extracting data without passwords to accessing cloud-based data from social media platforms – such as Instagram, X and Tinder – as well as data from connected devices such as Amazon’s Alexa and Google Home.

Experts argued that India’s current laws offer no guardrails against overreaching surveillance and the data extractions happen in a legal grey zone.

“It is clear that there is an expansion of India’s surveillance capabilities and it is becoming both wider and deeper,” said Vrinda Bhandari, a lawyer in the Supreme Court who works on digital rights and privacy issues.

“It’s now easier to conduct mass surveillance rather than targeted, specific surveillance and also possible to do more intrusive surveillance,” she told Al Jazeera. “[Today,] surveillance gives you a richer picture of an individual’s life.”

From Instagram to Tinder: Extracting cloud-based data

The IFF reviewed a letter also seen by Al Jazeera from India’s Ministry of Home Affairs dated January 7 in which Shah signed off on a wide-ranging, one-year waiver of “make in India” rules to clear a path for buying at least 422 forensic items.

Under “make in India” procurement rules, preference must be given to eligible Indian manufacturers over foreign suppliers in awarding government contracts. However, the rules allow exemptions with the approval of the minister in charge of the procuring department.

Another letter by the ministry dated January 20 showed Shah permitted the National Investigation Agency (NIA) to buy Israeli company Cellebrite’s Premium Tool on a three-year licence for about 50 million rupees ($529,947).

In specifications demanded by the government that were revealed in a review of tender bids, “solution” software must be capable of using login tokens recovered from seized phones or computers to access more than 100 cloud services. Login tokens are in effect digital keys that keep users signed in to online accounts.

Although an exemption for a company does not confirm whether a certain product was purchased by any government agency, it points to the range of forensic capabilities that opened up for procurement by Indian agencies.

From the 422-item exemption list, the IFF identified 118 items under digital and multimedia forensics, including Israeli company Cellebrite’s Pathfinder, Inseyets On-Prem Pro and Inseyets Offline.

Cellebrite’s tools have been used against journalists and activists in countries like Serbia, Jordan, Kenya and Russia.

Other products included tools from foreign digital-forensics companies like Magnet, MSAB, Oxygen Forensics and Belkasoft as well as software for open-source intelligence, dark-web monitoring and cryptocurrency investigations.

Al Jazeera reviewed a request for a bid proposal by the Delhi Police for software for its National Cyber Forensic Laboratory, which comes under the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre, an initiative of the Home Ministry.

Consider the capabilities the police department was seeking in its request: software that bypasses passwords on Apple’s macOS, Microsoft Windows and Linux operating systems; recovers internet activity, browser histories, deleted files and identifies traces of VPNs; bypasses screen locks; performs full file system extractions; decrypts backups; and extracts information from messaging applications.

The Delhi Police demanded another “all-in-one” system to access more than 100 cloud services, including Google, Apple, WhatsApp, Instagram, Telegram, Discord and dating platforms such as Tinder, Grindr and OkCupid or platforms like Slack and OnlyFans using account credentials or login tokens recovered from devices. Its specifications also sought the extraction of data from drones, wearable devices and devices like Amazon Alexa and Google Home.

Al Jazeera reached out to officials at the NIA, the Home Ministry and home departments of opposition-ruled states of Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka and Keralam for comments. The Delhi Police reports to Shah’s mInistry.

None of them had responded to Al Jazeera by the time of publication.

For some, the lack of transparency in the surveillance capabilities of India’s security agencies is not just a theoretical concern.

Last month, when Modi’s government faced street protests demanding the election chief resign, popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, a Modi critic, landed in New Delhi to participate in the demonstrations.

On the morning of the protest, he was detained by Delhi Police while still at home. His phone was taken from him. Speaking on a podcast later, Rathee said he believed police had tried to clone his iPhone using Israeli company Cellebrite’s tools but the attempt may have failed because his device was running a newer version of the iOS operating system than what the tool was capable of tricking.

Al Jazeera could not verify Rathee’s account, but Rathee is not alone in this suspicion.

Mohammad Aslam Hussain, a reporter with the newspaper Siasat Daily, told Al Jazeera that he was detained with a cameraperson on October 10 in New Delhi and his phone was confiscated at the scene.

“When I got my device later in the evening, all recorded footage of our reporting had been selectively deleted from the device,” Hussain said. The reporter uses Samsung’s Android-operated Galaxy S24 secured with a pattern lock and fingerprint authentication.

Hussain added that he cannot say conclusively what tools the police used to bypass his phone’s authentication requirement. “But it raises several questions with no one willing to respond to them,” he added. “How did they get inside my phone?”

The Indian government has faced accusations that it has used sophisticated spyware against journalists, activists, lawyers and political opponents during Modi’s years in power.

In 2019, WhatsApp disclosed that the Pegasus spyware, developed by the Israeli firm NSO Group, had been used to target Indian journalists and human rights defenders. Forensic examinations by Amnesty International later confirmed Pegasus infections on the phones of journalists Siddharth Varadarajan and Anand Mangnale. The government has denied allegations of unauthorised surveillance.

Bhandari told Al Jazeera that another problem in holding overarching surveillance to account is identifying the affected party. Often, she pointed out, the person placed under surveillance “does not know about it, so what does one do?”

The central legal gap identified by digital rights group IFF is that India has no statute or protocol that specifically authorises or regulates the forced unlocking and full extraction of data from a mobile phone seized by law enforcement agencies.

Existing seizure powers under criminal law do not explicitly address bypassing passcodes, copying an entire file system, harvesting login tokens to access cloud accounts or establishing rules for the retention and deletion of extracted data.

The Supreme Court in a 2017 judgement recognised privacy as a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution. The judgement established that any state intrusion into privacy must have a legal basis, pursue a legitimate state aim and be proportionate to that aim.

Bhandari told Al Jazeera that when the government agencies “deploy these capabilities without any proper meaningful oversight, the net of surveillance is cast wider and deeper and a lot more people are affected without either legislative, parliamentary or judicial oversight”.

Bhandari noted that while some countries like the United Kingdom or Germany “have some element of either parliamentary oversight or judicial oversight, India only has an internal review mechanism in executive oversight”.

“The whole point of having any oversight is to create a friction for surveillance,” she said, “so that it’s not easy for the government to just target everybody.”

“The current legal framework fails in this safeguard,” Bhandari said.
