articles.title: U.S. envoys in Moscow for meeting with Putin following talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s envoys arrived in Moscow on Thursday for talks with President Vladimir Putin about the results of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.
articles.body: President Donald Trump’s envoys arrived in Moscow on Thursday for talks with President Vladimir Putin about the results of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump’s son-in-law, attended the two days of negotiations in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. The talks wrapped up Wednesday with an agreement on a large exchange of prisoners, but no visible breakthrough on ending the nearly five-year hostilities. After meeting with Putin, Kushner said that he and Witkoff will fly to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Zelenskyy gave a muted welcome to the outcome of the talks, saying that the proposed prisoner exchange was a positive step. At the same time, he insisted that Ukraine won’t give in to demands that it cede its territory that has been occupied by Russia in exchange for peace. Hopes had been low for any significant breakthrough in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. From time to time, Russia and Ukraine have swapped prisoners, but have remained far apart in their demands for accepting a peace settlement. Along with post-conflict security guarantees for both countries, other key hurdles are the fate of Russia-occupied Ukrainian territory and what role European countries will play in an eventual settlement. Moscow doesn’t want European countries, which are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. Kushner said that one of the goals of the Moscow meeting is to try to get Europeans added to the talks. Kushner noted that both Ukraine and Russia needed clarity on post-conflict security arrangements, and European countries, the European Union and NATO have to be involved in those discussions to build consensus on the next steps. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that European representatives could eventually join peace talks. But Peskov said that their current statements “don’t indicate any desire on their part to contribute to movement along the path toward peace.” Moscow complains that Europe is financing and supplying weaponry to Ukraine. Ukraine wants to ensure that Moscow doesn’t attack again, and EU officials say any discussions on Europe’s security arrangements could only start after a ceasefire. Many in Europe see the inclusion of Russia in those plans as a concession to Putin, who has described NATO’s eastward expansion as a top security threat to his country. Moscow has demanded that the alliance withdraw its troops from Russia’s borders. Fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line, where little territory has changed hands this year, while both countries are battering each other with long-range missiles and drones. Russia’s Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. The ministry declared that the military has struck a drone-making plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital. It said that other strikes hit power substations in Zhytomyr and a bulk carrier heading to the Black Sea port of Odesa with cargo for the Ukrainian armed forces. A Russian military serviceman was killed in St. Petersburg early Thursday when his vehicle exploded, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee, the country’s main criminal investigation agency. It didn’t name the victim or say who could be behind the bombing. Fontanka news outlet said that the victim was a colonel and an explosive device in his car went off as he drove off. Another person accompanying him was wounded, it said. Several senior officers have been killed by bombings and other attacks that Russia has blamed on Ukraine. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some attacks on Russian soil.

articles.title: US envoys arrive in Moscow for Russia-Ukraine talks with Putin
articles.summary: The meeting with Kushner and Witkoff comes after two days of trilateral talks in the UAE yielded no breakthrough.
articles.body:
United States envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have ⁠arrived in ⁠Moscow for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in their latest push for a peace deal ⁠in Ukraine.

Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy, met Kushner and Witkoff at their plane on Thursday morning and accompanied them to central Moscow.

The meeting comes on the heels of two days of trilateral peace talks in the United Arab Emirates that concluded in the capital, Abu Dhabi, on Wednesday with news of another planned major prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the nearly five-year war.

The US said differences remained on major issues, including territory, but some progress had been made on post-war security guarantees.

Kyiv has strongly rejected Putin’s demands to surrender all of its eastern region of Donbas in ⁠return for peace.

The Abu Dhabi talks were the first direct negotiations between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the US in nine months.

Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said one of the goals of Thursday’s visit would be for the US team to persuade Putin to invite Europeans to the negotiation process .

“Ukraine and the US want the European partners to be involved while Moscow is adamant about talks without the Europeans, and that’s why they’ve been largely excluded from the process,” she said.

Shapovalova added that the US delegation would bring Putin an updated proposal for a peace plan and the presence of Dmitriev in the talks was an indication that they would address some of the more complex issues.

During the US-backed effort to revive talks, leaders from more than 40 European countries gathered in Dublin on Thursday for a summit focused on the continent’s security.

The meeting of the European Political Community (EPC) brought together heads of state and government from the European Union and other European countries, including the United Kingdom. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte also attended.

The EPC was established in 2022 as a forum for countries both inside and outside the 27-nation EU.

Zelenskyy and his European allies are expected to discuss this week’s talks in Abu Dhabi.

Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, and Witkoff are scheduled to meet Zelenskyy in Dublin on Friday after talking to Putin.

Audrey Macalpine, reporting from Kyiv, said Ukrainians do not believe the talks in Moscow will yield results. “Over the past two days, we saw just another prisoner exchange, which has been the case in previous talks,” the correspondent said.

“When it comes to the negotiations, not much has changed in terms of where these two sides stand,” Macalpine added. “Perhaps the biggest thing of note [in the talks] was that they took place at all.”

Meanwhile, French Minister Delegate for European Affairs Benjamin Haddad on Thursday ‌said the ⁠EU will approve more sanctions ⁠against Russia.

“On Monday, we will take new sanctions against ⁠Russia on 150 additional ⁠entities, 50 banks, and it’s ⁠France which proposed the ⁠bulk ⁠of the entities to add,” Haddad ‌told LCI television.

articles.title: Romanov sapphire worn by Russian empress fetches $4.9M at auction
articles.summary: A Romanov sapphire weighing nearly 198 carats on a diamond-covered bracelet sold for more than 4.1 million Swiss francs ($4.9 million) at auction.
articles.body: A Romanov sapphire weighing nearly 198 carats on a diamond-covered bracelet sold for more than 4.1 million Swiss francs ($4.9 million) at auction, vastly higher than the expected price range, Sotheby’s said. The cushion-shaped sapphire attributed to onetime ownership of Russia’s imperial family was billed as a very rare stone, and had been expected to fetch between 850,000 and 1.7 million francs ($1 million and $2 million) at the Geneva auction late Wednesday. The buyer, a private collector, wasn’t identified. The 197.80-carat Ceylon sapphire likely came from the Mughal Empire in south Asia, made its way into Russia’s imperial jewels in the 19th century and is one of the most important surviving gemstones from the Russian court. Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna, Czar Nicholas II’s mother, wore the sapphire at the Winter Palace Ball of 1903 — “widely regarded as the last great spectacle of Imperial Russia and immortalized in some of the most iconic images of the Romanov court,” the auction house said. After the Russian Revolution, the sapphire was recorded in inventory before entering the Soviet government’s dispersal sales of imperial treasures, Sotheby’s said.

articles.title: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.summary: An Israeli airstrike on a hospital in southern Gaza overnight killed at least six people, the health ministry in the Palestinian enclave said Thursday.
articles.body: An Israeli airstrike on a hospital in southern Gaza overnight killed at least six people, the health ministry in the Palestinian enclave said Thursday. The strike hit a surgery building at Nasser Hospital, with medical staff and patients among those killed, the health ministry said. The Israeli military said it was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants. The strike — the latest despite an ongoing U.S.-backed ceasefire — shattered ceilings and left debris strewn across rooms inside the hospital, which is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza after the destruction of Israel’s yearslong assault. Palestinian surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira was among those killed, the health ministry said. He was featured in the 2026 documentary “American Doctor,” which followed three American doctors helping to provide medical care in Gaza. Watermelon Pictures, which distributed the film, said it was “devastating by the killing” of the surgeon. Its thoughts were with the surgeon’s loved ones and colleagues, the company said in a statement published on social media Thursday morning, as it condemned the attack “and the continued assault on Gaza’s healthcare system.” The Israeli military and Israel Security Agency said they struck a senior Hamas member, along with other militants, who they said had “advanced” attacks from the hospital in the southern Gaza Strip overnight. In a later statement, they identified the senior member as Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom they said served as the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade and had also been responsible for holding hostages in Gaza. The IDF and ISA said Hamas had “established a presence within the hospital complex and used it as a command center” and stored weapons and conducted interrogations and torture from within the medical complex. They shared photos of weapons alleged to have been found within the complex. Hamas condemned the allegations that it was using the hospital for military operations as “lies of the criminal enemy” and called the attack a “war crime.” The Israel Defense Forces and ISA said steps had been taken to “mitigate harm to civilians, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance.” The IDF said it was looking into reports that medical workers, including Abu Shaira, and patients were killed. Hospitals have protected status under international law, but they have been heavily targeted under Israel’s yearslong offensive in Gaza. The Israeli military has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating within medical facilities, a charge the militant group has denied. The overnight attack was not the first time that Nasser Hospital itself has been targeted. In August 2025, the hospital was hit by a double tap Israeli strike that killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers. The deadly attack sparked international outrage. Of Gaza’s 37 hospitals, just 2 are considered to be “fully functioning,” while 18 are partially functioning and 17 are considered non-functioning after much of the enclave’s healthcare system was devastated under Israel’s offensive, according to data published by the World Health Organization. Israeli strikes have continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreement reached in October of last year. More than 1,600 people have been killed since the truce came into effect, according to the Palestinian health ministry in the enclave. Israel says four of its ⁠soldiers have ​been killed in that time. Both Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire. More than 74,600 people, including thousands of children, have been killed overall in Gaza since Israel launched its offensive in the enclave following the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attacks, in which some 1,200 people were killed and around 250 taken hostage. The latest strikes come as Palestinians contend with heavy rains and desperate conditions in the enclave as the colder months set in, prompting a fresh wave of outcry over the lack of progress in advancing the peace deal between Israel and Hamas.

articles.title: The man who makes millionaires wait for their Land Rovers
articles.summary: Prices start at $224,000 and the waiting list is 3 years. Inside the Lisbon warehouse where vintage Land Rovers are reborn.
articles.body: There is a commanding photograph of an oversized golden screw hanging on the wall in Ricardo Pessoa’s office. It is strangely beautiful and perfectly in keeping with the atmosphere he has created in the warehouse of Coolnvintage (CNV), the unique business he runs in Lisbon, Portugal. The company’s website provides little detail of what it offers, and certainly no information about how much it costs to undertake one of its projects. But that is part of the point. Pessoa takes on 12 clients a year, 14 at most. The waiting list is up to three years long and not just anyone can join. The clue, however, is in the bio of CNV’s Instagram page: “Painstakingly restoring Land Rovers with an obsession for detail and a commitment to the essentials.” Here, in a former Xerox facility in an eastern suburb of the city, Pessoa and his team bring road-weary Land Rovers back to life and elevate them to works of art. The cavernous workshop is a far cry from your local garage. Pessoa’s Bernese mountain dog Alfie surveys the scene from the mezzanine, where his owner is currently working on a soon-to-publish book of adventure photography. Music, kept at a low level, is interrupted only by the sound of power tools as members of Pessoa’s 17-strong team devote fanatical attention to the task in hand. The space is filled with Land Rovers in various states – some disassembled, some overhauled and some which Pessoa has not yet worked out what to do with. Each renovation begins by completely disassembling the car and 3D scanning all the parts which are then restored, replaced or stored for future builds in the meticulously catalogued warehouse. “A car takes 1,200 different parts, not counting bolts, screws, washers and all these consumables, so in total maybe 3,000,” said Pessoa. “We check every part three times.” Meticulous mechanics Established in 2012, CNV was initially more a labor of love than a livelihood. “I traveled a lot with Land Rovers when I was younger,” Pessoa said. “I bought one, started doing some trips in Portugal and then gathered the courage to go to Morocco, Guinea, Angola… I’ve done most of Africa although unfortunately never in one trip.” He would fix up the vehicle before each adventure. “People loved the cars so I would sell them when I got back, before going on to do the next one and the next one.” He later employed professionals for the restorations but remained “very hands-on,” operating out of smaller premises while keeping his day job running a media business. Eventually Pessoa decided to focus solely on CNV and moved to this warehouse in 2022. Today CNV has almost 400,000 followers on Instagram and demand for their cars far outstrips supply. The firm has only ever restored 200 Land Rovers, with each project requiring an average of 2,000 hours skilled labor. “I don’t want to scale the business by any means,” said Pessoa. “I don’t want to just do the product and say, ‘give me the money for the car’ and that’s it, so I get to choose people I feel we’re in sync with.” That can –– and has –– meant turning away business from “people who aren’t looking for what we can offer,” he admitted. “I steer them to different companies who I think could do a better job.” Scouring the globe Launched in Britain in the 1940s, the 4x4’s mission was, as the name suggests, to “rove the land, regardless of conditions.” “They were made for agriculture and military purposes and to work on farms and many did,” said Pessoa. As such, the vehicles were never designed with comfort and mod cons in mind. “As we go to more autonomous driving and AI, a lot of people are trying to hold on to this,” he said. “Everything is very mechanical. It gives you more of a sense of being alive. Special technology removes all this from your life –– you take everything for granted.” Driving these Land Rovers “really slows you down,” he added. “You want to make a call? Forget about it, too noisy. You don’t even hear the phone ringing.” Almost two thirds of customers commission renovations of vehicles they already own, including those looking to revitalize Land Rovers which might have spent years neglected within their families. Others entrust Pessoa to source the Land Rover. “Sometimes it takes three months and sometimes it takes two years,” he said. “We have a huge network and people know us from socials. If we do a story saying we’re looking for such a car we get flooded with messages.” Portugal is a “very Land Rover heavy country,” but Pessoa travels to every corner of the globe in search of the perfect vehicle, which includes researching its history and provenance. “We bring them from everywhere, even New Zealand,” he said. “It’s very typical that I land somewhere, rent a car, have an address, put it in the GPS. The last ten miles might be on a dirt track, with the Land Rover in a shed somewhere. “It’s really cool going to new places which you would never go to in your life and then to meet these people who say, ‘it was in a really great condition when I parked it here 35 years ago.’” If the vehicle fits the bill, Pessoa informs the client who makes the purchase and arranges shipment to Lisbon. Needless to say, CNV restorations do not come cheap, with projects starting at 200,000 euros ($224,000) –– excluding the cost of the vehicle and “logistics.” ‘The timeline is a kind of goal’ Pessoa’s current favorite is a “patina project” –– meaning the original paintwork remains, complete with faded scratches –– for a UK client who already owns five others. Pessoa himself owns “around ten,” yet he flinches at the suggestion that either of them is a collector. “The difference between a collector and someone who has a few but doesn’t collect is usage,” he explained. “A collector would have all the cars together because they want to see them and they’re collecting because of specs or year or color. I don’t want people to have it so they can tell people they have it.” His customers are “not afraid of abusing” the vehicles, he said. “Our Land Rovers are meant to be driven not collected. For me, that’s the most important part of the company’s DNA.” His clients are predominantly male, though a growing number of women now buy from him too. They are mostly CEOs, former CEOs or founders of big companies. “I’m getting them at the best stage of their lives,” said Pessoa, 47. “They’re at the point which I’m now getting to, where you realize your own mortality and think ‘I need to start enjoying myself.’” Pessoa meets every prospective client before signing a contract, which usually means welcoming them to Lisbon for a “very special and organized visit.” He explained: “I have an old Rolls Royce from 1971, a Silver Shadow. We pick them up from the airport in it and take care of them.” They maintain a close relationship throughout the process, with Pessoa keeping clients abreast of significant developments. He has been known to send clients artistic photos of small components (hence the golden screw shot), and once made a record of an engine for its music-loving owner. Given the price tag, one might expect clients to call the shots. Not so fast. “I’m the author,” said Pessoa. “I know very well what they like and what I think they should have so we kind of negotiate, but it’s not something they come here to choose,” he said of details such as paintwork. The same goes for any kind of ETA. “The timeline is a kind of goal,” he said. “It will be ready when I think it’s done.” Once complete, Pessoa either personally delivers the Land Rover or arranges the handover at one of two luxury retreats in Portugal and Morocco. “If it’s a car I bought for you and you don’t forge some sort of relationship with it, it’s just a car,” he said. “They need to get this connection so I leave them alone for two or three days so they can do the first drives with their family. They have the kids in the back, they go for a picnic, they go horse riding. They’ll always remember this.” This is how client Nuno Ventura took ownership of one of his two restored Land Rovers. “That made receiving the car something very special. The setting, the attention, the personal involvement –– it all became part of the memory of the car.” Patiently awaiting completion of his third vehicle, Ventura said the aspect of the restoration he is most impressed with is “how much of himself Ricardo puts into every project.” “When you spend between 200,000 and 300,000 euros and wait a year-and-a-half to two years, you have very high expectations,” he added. “The quality of the restoration is essential, but so is the relationship throughout that time.”

articles.title: From the UK to the Gulf, are US overseas bases becoming liabilities?
articles.summary: For decades, these bases allowed the US to wage faraway wars. Now, Iran has changed that calculation.
articles.body:
Doha, Qatar — Late one morning in March 1999, a United States B-52 bomber took off from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, headed southeast. Seven more jets followed, at two-minute intervals.

It was the start of the US-led NATO bombing of Yugoslavia, a campaign in which the Fairford base served as both a pivotal launchpad for American jets and as a fuel station for fighter planes. The British base had served a similar role during the Gulf War in 1991, and would do so again during the 2003 Iraq war and in the early stages of the US-Israeli war on Iran that began on February 28, 2026.

But in October, the US pulled all 12 of its B-1 Lancer bombers from the Gloucestershire base, amid fears that they were no longer safe there from a growing Iranian threat. Days earlier, British security forces had made several arrests, and the country’s government has accused Iran of being behind a plot to target the base — a charge Tehran has denied.

RAF Fairford is not alone. Earlier this month, the US withdrew a dozen planes from another British base, RAF Mildenhall. And in July, reports said that the US had relocated many of its military assets from its bases in the Gulf that were badly hit by Iran during the war, instead moving them to bases in Jordan, while also considering a proposal to shift them to Israel.

For decades, these bases have served as the sharp edge of the US military’s ability to project power and wage wars thousands of miles from home. For close allies, whether in Europe or the Gulf, they also worked as security guarantors against other threats.

But Iran’s ability to severely damage US facilities in the Middle East during the war, and pose a threat as far as the UK, has for the first time turned these critical strategic assets into potential liabilities, both for American allies and for the US itself, say analysts.

“The US security umbrella is becoming a double-edged sword,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera. “When the security of US bases is called into question, it changes Washington’s calculation of their strategic benefits. It also gives European and Gulf states reason to think seriously about the bases, given that they are becoming targets.”

Hosting American bases has long been perceived as integral to how US allies, whether in Europe, the Gulf or East Asia, deter threats that they themselves face.

Former US President Barack Obama once spoke of an “ironclad commitment” to Gulf security, while Britain regularly invokes its so-called “special relationship” with the United States. In doing so, Britain and the Gulf have long cast themselves as willing partners to a power that — at least before current President Donald Trump — presented itself as the benevolent guarantor of its allies’ security.

But a spate of recent security incidents, many linked to the war on Iran, is testing that narrative and raising questions about whose interests these commitments serve, and whether hosting American forces could be bringing danger closer to home.

US prosecutors have charged three men they describe as Iranian-backed operatives over their alleged roles in plotting nearly 20 attacks across the United States and Europe, including on RAF Fairford.

Meanwhile, in the Gulf, Iran explicitly cited the presence of US bases as justification for targeting its neighbours, bombing Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Kuwait. Iran also bombed Oman, which does not have a permanent US base; and Jordan and Iraq, beyond the Gulf, which do host major US military facilities.

A report by the Pentagon’s watchdog released in September revealed that Iranian attacks damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US military installations in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan in the first four months of the war.

At least five KC-135 aerial refuelling tankers were damaged when they were hit at the Prince Sultan airbase in Saudi Arabia. At least one of these airborne early-warning and control aircraft was damaged on the ground in a subsequent strike.

Experts say these incidents are sharpening a security dilemma for US allies in the Gulf and Europe. Hosting US forces can expose them to retaliation in a war they had no say in starting, while those same bases help defend some of those host countries from attacks, including by intercepting missiles and providing weapons transfers.

The war has disrupted flights and shipping, threatening the oil and gas exports on which much of the region depends. US President Donald Trump said on Monday that further military action against Iran was unnecessary for now. But the US naval blockade remains in place, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has yet to return to normal.

“While the utility of hosting foreign military bases has always involved a calculus of risk versus the assumed assurance it provides, the perception among Gulf Arab states is certainly shifting,” Mohammad Ali Shabani, a Middle East analyst, told Al Jazeera. “The vulnerability of these assets is increasingly front-of-mind for host governments, who have not sought war, yet have been drawn into it without having had any real say.”

Washington faces a dilemma of its own. Bases in Europe or the Middle East give it the reach to fight faraway wars, but their presence has also provided Iran with a litany of targets.

In March, an Iranian drone hit a hangar at a British base in Cyprus that the US also uses for intelligence and logistics operations. Tehran threatened Bulgaria after reports emerged that the Eastern European NATO nation had allowed the US to use its Bezmer airbase for refuelling of planes used to attack Iran. Weeks later, Bulgaria’s defence minister announced that the US air tankers had left Bezmer for good, with the country’s president declaring that the “mission is over,” bringing relief to the village that the base draws its name from.

And in the Middle East, several key bases used by US troops have been almost rendered unusable, with those in Kuwait suffering the heaviest damage, say analysts. An attack on the Port of Shuaiba killed six US service members and destroyed an army operations centre. Iranian drones and missiles damaged aviation facilities and injured personnel at Ali Al Salem airbase, while strikes on Camp Buehring damaged maintenance and refuelling facilities.

In Qatar, an Iranian strike damaged the early warning radar system at Al Udeid airbase, which houses the headquarters of US Central Command’s (CENTCOM) air operations. In Bahrain, an Iranian drone struck communications equipment at the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet.

This damage raises a question about how much the US can still use these bases once they come under attack. Gerd Nonneman, a professor of international relations and Gulf studies at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera the war had shown that some bases were “themselves very vulnerable” and “unable to fulfil many of the tasks they were established for”.

Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer at the Defence Studies Department at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera “large bases are indeed becoming more easily targeted”.

“One of the technologies that has allowed this, alongside fairly cheap ballistic missiles, is drones,” he added.

Iran has invested heavily in developing cheap, domestically produced drones that inflict disproportionate damage to targets and exhaust far more expensive interceptor missiles.

Meanwhile in the UK, drones present US airbases with different challenges. While the nature of the reported threat to RAF Mildenhall remains unclear, the Fairford case concerns an alleged plot. “The range of actors who might target bases has changed,” Urban Coningham, a research fellow and course lead at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) in the UK, told Al Jazeera. “Bases are more vulnerable, and that changes the risk calculation.

“Anyone can manufacture a drone in a basement … People looking to create mischief or mayhem can recruit organised criminals, making attacks harder to attribute.”

All of that, he said, makes bases “more vulnerable, and that changes the risk calculation”.

As Washington moves some military assets out of bases in the Gulf and Europe, it could also come to rely more heavily on Israel, its closest ally in the Middle East. Shabani said there were “already signs that CENTCOM is moving towards using Israel as a key forward base”.

Israel launched the war on Iran in February alongside the US. With the oil and gas exports on which Gulf economies depend at risk, keeping US forces nearby allows Washington to respond, but it also leaves those forces exposed to Iranian attacks.

“The longer-term solution is to work with partners and ensure that allied forces are ready to fend for themselves,” RUSI’s Coningham said.

“There is a debate within the US policy establishment, and the Iranians are referencing it and saying that as long as US forces are there, they are a target,” he said. “That is the policy conundrum for the US. Ultimately, they can’t see any alternative to having bases in some form.”

articles.title: Ukraine says Starshield is being limited again, hampering its defenses against Russia
articles.summary: The Ukrainian military has experienced a renewed wave of “significant disruptions” to the Starshield satellite internet service, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday, hampering its ability to defend against Russia.
articles.body: The Ukrainian military has experienced a renewed wave of “significant disruptions” to the Starshield satellite internet service, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday, hampering its ability to defend against Russia. Units have for several days reported speed restrictions affecting the entire front line and Russian-occupied parts of the country, Zelenskyy said in a social media post. A limit of 100 miles per hour is “being imposed on Starshield,” Zelenskyy said of the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink communications service. “These are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions,” Zelenskyy said. “For us, this primarily means a significant complication in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones.” The system normally runs at a stable speed exceeding around 250 miles per hour. “Unfortunately, there have already been strikes that got through because our interception systems cannot reach sufficient speeds and are unable to intercept in time,” he said, adding that Ukraine was trying to ⁠clarify the reasons for the ‌restriction with the ​U.S. side. Ukraine first raised the alarm last month about speed limits being imposed on Starshield, which is crucial to its battlefield operations and air defenses. Starlink owner Elon Musk put the responsibility for the restrictions on Trump, who has been trying to pressure Kyiv to make concessions to end the war. The U.S. government said ​that any such decision could only have been ‌taken by Musk. Trump denied being involved in the decision concerning the slowdown. The renewed issues came as U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were in Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin, a day after trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Abu Dhabi.
